passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted even by treaty — occupies an uneasy position within international law. Unlike ordinary customary international law, which states may contract out of by persistent objection, jus cogens norms bind all states unconditionally and void any treaty provision inconsistent with them. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, adopted in 1969, formally codified this concept in Articles 53 and 64, yet the Convention offered no enumerated list of which norms qualify as peremptory. The result is a doctrinal lacuna that national and international tribunals have struggled, with uneven success, to fill.

The principal difficulty lies in the identification criterion. Most international law scholars accept that a norm attains peremptory status when it is recognized by the international community of states as a whole as admitting of no exception. This formulation, however, is notoriously circular: a norm is peremptory because states say it is, but states claim it is peremptory only when the norm already enjoys near-universal acceptance. In practice, tribunals invoking jus cogens have relied on what might be called the gravity heuristic — the proposition that norms prohibiting the most severe violations of human dignity, such as the prohibition on torture and the prohibition on slavery, are self-evidently peremptory. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion issued in 1996 endorsed this heuristic when it declined to specify a complete list but noted that prohibitions on genocide and on crimes against humanity were of unquestionable peremptory character. Yet the gravity heuristic yields indeterminate answers at the margins. In a 2003 arbitral proceeding, a European state attempted to invoke jus cogens to defeat a bilateral investment treaty's expropriation clause, arguing that systematic economic deprivation constituted a violation of peremptory norms against exploitation. The tribunal rejected the claim, holding that the norm alleged was insufficiently crystallized, but offered no principled basis for distinguishing crystallized from uncrystallized norms beyond a vague appeal to state practice.

The problem is compounded when lex specialis is introduced. Lex specialis — the principle that a more specific rule prevails over a general one within the same legal system — operates, in ordinary treaty regimes, to displace general customary rules. But jus cogens, precisely because it is hierarchically superior to ordinary treaty law, should in theory be immune to lex specialis displacement. Whether it actually is in practice remains contested. When specialized regimes such as the World Trade Organization dispute-settlement system or bilateral investment-treaty arbitration are invoked, the applicable procedural rules make no express provision for jus cogens defenses, and arbitral panels have shown considerable reluctance to entertain them, frequently ruling that such defenses fall outside their jurisdictional mandate. This reluctance is understandable as a matter of institutional self-restraint, but it has the unfortunate effect of allowing states to structure specialized adjudicatory forums in ways that effectively insulate treaty obligations from peremptory-norm review. One hopes that future reform of international adjudicatory architecture will address this structural evasion more directly, for the integrity of jus cogens as a meaningful constraint on state conduct depends on there being no safe harbor in which treaty obligations contrary to peremptory norms may be enforced with impunity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered jus cogens unenforceable in contemporary international law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because jus cogens norms lack a reliable identification criterion and face structural evasion in specialized adjudicatory forums, their effectiveness as a genuine constraint on state conduct is seriously imperiled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gravity heuristic, though imperfect, provides the most workable standard for identifying jus cogens norms and should be adopted by international tribunals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The principle of lex specialis is fundamentally incompatible with peremptory norms and should be abolished within international treaty regimes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International tribunals have been inconsistent in their application of jus cogens primarily because states have not agreed on a list of norms qualifying as peremptory.

explanations.correct: The passage traces two compounding problems — the circularity of the identification criterion (paragraph 2) and the structural evasion enabled by specialized forums (paragraph 3) — and culminates in the normative claim that jus cogens as a 'meaningful constraint' is threatened by both. B integrates these two strands.
explanations.A: Too strong and too narrow: the passage does not say jus cogens is 'unenforceable,' and does not attribute all problems solely to the Vienna Convention's omission.
explanations.C: The passage treats the gravity heuristic skeptically ('yields indeterminate answers at the margins') and does not endorse it as the best available standard.
explanations.D: The passage never calls for abolition of lex specialis; it argues only that jus cogens should be immune to lex specialis displacement, a narrower point.
explanations.E: This captures the identification-criterion problem of paragraph 2 but ignores the equally prominent forum-evasion problem of paragraph 3, making it too narrow.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced; its formal codification is described; a counterargument to its validity is presented; and a proposal for its abolition is advanced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is situated within international law; the primary difficulty in applying it is identified and illustrated with a case example; a second, compounding difficulty is introduced; and the author expresses concern about the doctrine's viability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; two judicial decisions endorsing it are examined; a scholarly debate about its scope is surveyed; and a preferred scholarly view is endorsed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tension between two competing legal principles is established; the historical origins of each are traced; their incompatibility is demonstrated through case analysis; and a legislative solution is recommended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its key identification criterion is described; the criterion's limitations are acknowledged; and a different doctrine is proposed as superior.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 situates jus cogens within international law and notes its codification gap; paragraph 2 identifies the identification-criterion difficulty and illustrates it with the 1996 ICJ opinion and 2003 arbitral proceeding; paragraph 3 introduces the compounding lex specialis/forum-evasion problem; and the closing sentences express the author's concern. B maps these moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not present a counterargument to jus cogens' validity, nor does it propose abolition.
explanations.C: Only one judicial decision (1996 ICJ advisory opinion) is examined in detail, not two; and no 'preferred scholarly view' is explicitly endorsed beyond the author's closing hope.
explanations.D: The passage does not trace the historical origins of both jus cogens and lex specialis, and no legislative solution is recommended.
explanations.E: The passage does not propose a different doctrine as superior to jus cogens; it advocates for better adjudicatory architecture to protect jus cogens.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion did which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enumerated a complete list of norms qualifying as jus cogens in order to resolve the doctrinal lacuna left by the Vienna Convention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Explicitly endorsed the lex specialis principle as applicable within jus cogens disputes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Declined to provide an exhaustive list of peremptory norms but affirmed that prohibitions on genocide and crimes against humanity unquestionably qualified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Held that systematic economic deprivation constituted a violation of peremptory norms against exploitation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversed the earlier position of the Vienna Convention by requiring states to reach unanimous agreement before a norm could be deemed peremptory.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the 1996 ICJ advisory opinion 'declined to specify a complete list but noted that prohibitions on genocide and on crimes against humanity were of unquestionable peremptory character.' C is a precise paraphrase.
explanations.A: The opposite of what the passage states: the opinion explicitly declined to provide a complete list.
explanations.B: The passage does not attribute any position on lex specialis to the 1996 advisory opinion.
explanations.D: This describes the claim made by the European state in the 2003 arbitral proceeding, not the 1996 ICJ opinion.
explanations.E: The passage makes no mention of the ICJ reversing the Vienna Convention's position, nor of a unanimity requirement.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the 2003 arbitral tribunal's decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was legally incorrect because systematic economic deprivation does qualify as a violation of a peremptory norm against exploitation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reached an acceptable outcome in rejecting the jus cogens defense but failed to provide an adequate principled basis for that rejection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It demonstrated that bilateral investment treaties are inherently incompatible with peremptory norms and should be renegotiated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It was the inevitable result of the Vienna Convention's decision to codify jus cogens without supplying an enumerated list.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It correctly applied the gravity heuristic by finding that economic deprivation, however severe, cannot rise to the level of a peremptory norm violation.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the tribunal's ruling as holding that the claimed norm was 'insufficiently crystallized' but notes the tribunal 'offered no principled basis for distinguishing crystallized from uncrystallized norms.' The author's implicit criticism is one of methodological inadequacy, not necessarily of the outcome itself. B captures this.
explanations.A: The author does not affirm that systematic economic deprivation qualifies as a peremptory-norm violation; the passage presents this as an open question.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest bilateral investment treaties are inherently incompatible with jus cogens, nor does it recommend renegotiation.
explanations.D: The passage presents the Vienna Convention's lack of a list as one contributing factor to doctrinal uncertainty, but does not characterize the 2003 ruling as its inevitable result.
explanations.E: The passage notes the tribunal rejected the claim without endorsing the gravity heuristic, and the author does not credit the tribunal with correctly applying any particular standard.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the gravity heuristic (second paragraph) serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Propose a definitive method for resolving disputes about which norms qualify as peremptory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Illustrate both the partial utility and the critical limitation of the approach that tribunals have in practice adopted to identify jus cogens norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contrast the ICJ's methodology with that of arbitral panels to show that international courts apply jus cogens more rigorously.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Demonstrate that the Vienna Convention's codification of jus cogens was itself an application of the gravity heuristic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Provide an example of how lex specialis operates to displace general customary norms in specialized treaty regimes.

explanations.correct: The gravity heuristic is introduced as the approach tribunals have relied upon in practice, the ICJ opinion is cited to show its partial acceptance, and then the 2003 arbitral proceeding is cited to illustrate that it 'yields indeterminate answers at the margins.' The function is to present a real but insufficient solution to the identification problem. B captures this dual role.
explanations.A: The passage treats the gravity heuristic as imperfect, not definitive — the very next sentence calls it indeterminate at the margins.
explanations.C: The passage does not draw a methodological contrast between ICJ and arbitral panels in the second paragraph; the 2003 arbitral proceeding is used to illustrate the heuristic's limitations, not to compare it favorably or unfavorably with ICJ methodology.
explanations.D: The passage does not attribute the Vienna Convention's codification to the gravity heuristic.
explanations.E: Lex specialis is not introduced until the third paragraph; it plays no role in the second paragraph's discussion.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reluctance of arbitral panels to entertain jus cogens defenses can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete condemnation, because such reluctance reveals the bad faith of states that design specialized forums to evade peremptory norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Unqualified approval, because institutional self-restraint prevents tribunals from overstepping their jurisdictional mandates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sympathetic understanding of the institutional rationale paired with clear concern about the structural consequence for the integrity of jus cogens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mild skepticism that such reluctance is as widespread as critics claim, given the existence of robust international human rights mechanisms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resigned acceptance that the current adjudicatory architecture is permanently inadequate and cannot be reformed.

explanations.correct: The author explicitly states that arbitral panels' reluctance is 'understandable as a matter of institutional self-restraint' — the sympathetic acknowledgment — but immediately adds 'it has the unfortunate effect of allowing states to structure specialized forums in ways that effectively insulate treaty obligations from peremptory-norm review' — the concern. C captures both valences precisely.
explanations.A: Too strong; the author acknowledges the legitimacy of institutional self-restraint and does not impute bad faith to states.
explanations.B: Too one-sided; the author explicitly characterizes the consequence as 'unfortunate,' signaling disapproval of the outcome even while understanding the rationale.
explanations.D: The passage makes no mention of critics' claims about how widespread the reluctance is, nor of human rights mechanisms as a counterweight.
explanations.E: The author's closing 'one hopes' sentence expresses optimism about future reform, directly contradicting resigned acceptance.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that specialized adjudicatory forums allow states to effectively insulate treaty obligations from peremptory-norm review?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several bilateral investment treaties concluded after 2005 contain express clauses requiring arbitral panels to consider jus cogens defenses before rendering awards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gravity heuristic has been criticized by a majority of international law scholars as an insufficiently rigorous standard for identifying peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties has never been ratified by some of the world's most powerful states.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arbitral panels operating under bilateral investment treaties have issued awards that rely on customary international law principles distinct from jus cogens.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International human rights tribunals have consistently held that prohibitions on torture and genocide qualify as peremptory norms under jus cogens.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that states can design specialized forums to insulate treaty obligations from jus cogens review, and that arbitral panels disclaim jurisdictional competence over such defenses. If bilateral investment treaties themselves expressly require arbitral panels to consider jus cogens defenses, the mechanism of evasion the author identifies is directly undermined. A targets the load-bearing claim.
explanations.B: This concerns the gravity heuristic's scholarly reception, not the forum-evasion claim; it actually tends to support the author's broader skepticism about identification without weakening the structural-evasion argument.
explanations.C: Non-ratification by powerful states is a separate problem concerning the Convention's reach, not the insulation mechanism within forums that do apply the Convention's framework.
explanations.D: Reliance on customary international law distinct from jus cogens neither confirms nor denies that jus cogens defenses are being excluded; it is largely neutral with respect to the author's specific claim.
explanations.E: This confirms that certain norms are peremptory but does not address whether specialized forums permit or exclude jus cogens defenses — it is off-target relative to the forum-evasion claim.
